concepts.title: अहम् — I

explanations.kidFriendly: In Sanskrit, 'I' is अहम् — pronounced aham. This word belongs to the Pronouns group, so you'll meet it again when you study other words in the same family. Try saying it out loud: aham.
explanations.textbook: अहम् (aham). First person singular pronoun, nominative case. In Hindi this corresponds to मैं; in English, 'I'.
explanations.expert: First person singular pronoun, nominative case. Words in the Pronouns category share patterns of declension or usage — comparing अहम् with other entries in the same category will reveal the underlying paradigm. The transliteration aham uses IAST conventions: long vowels are marked with a macron (ā, ī, ū), and retroflex sounds with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ).

concepts.reasoning: In Sanskrit, 'I' is rendered as अहम् (aham). First person singular pronoun, nominative case.

concepts.title: अतीव — very / much

explanations.kidFriendly: In Sanskrit, 'very / much' is अतीव — pronounced atīva. This word belongs to the Particles group, so you'll meet it again when you study other words in the same family. Try saying it out loud: atīva.
explanations.textbook: अतीव (atīva). Indeclinable adverb of degree. In Hindi this corresponds to बहुत; in English, 'very / much'.
explanations.expert: Indeclinable adverb of degree. Words in the Particles category share patterns of declension or usage — comparing अतीव with other entries in the same category will reveal the underlying paradigm. The transliteration atīva uses IAST conventions: long vowels are marked with a macron (ā, ī, ū), and retroflex sounds with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ).

concepts.reasoning: In Sanskrit, 'very / much' is rendered as अतीव (atīva). Indeclinable adverb of degree.

useCases.title: Hear it in conversation
useCases.description: When someone says 'atīva' in a Sanskrit conversation, they mean 'very / much'.
